result: Neural responses in ferret auditory cortex and human MEG show localized adaptation to contextual Shepard tone sequences. The adaptation is frequency-specific, builds up over ~3-5 stimuli, reduces responses by 13-33% in the adapted region, and recovers with a time constant of ~1.2 seconds. This adaptation is consistent with stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA) and matches between ferret single-unit and human MEG recordings.
evaluation: All three reviewers accept these findings without challenge. The editor describes the data as 'convincing single-neuron data and analyses,' Reviewer 1 states 'experimental design and data collection appear to have been executed carefully,' and Reviewer 2 notes 'the methods seem sound and the conclusions warranted.' The consistency between ferret and human data strengthens the findings.

result: Decoding analysis using direction-selective cells successfully predicts the context-dependent percept of ambiguous tritone pairs. Cells with directional tuning (ascending vs. descending preference) show differential activity patterns that correlate with the perceptual bias induced by the contextual sequence, with statistical significance (p=0.03 for neural data, p<0.001 for model).
evaluation: Reviewers accept this as a key finding. The editor notes the study 'demonstrates convincingly that traditional neural decoding models cannot explain percepts' and that the direction-aware approach provides an alternative. Reviewer 1 states 'the conclusion that traditional decoding models cannot explain the contextual effects on percepts is quite strong,' implicitly accepting the directional decoding results. Reviewer 2 calls the study 'elegant' and finds the case 'fairly convincing.'

result: Traditional pitch-class decoding based on minimal distance in circular Shepard tone space predicts the opposite of the actual percept. The neural representation shows repulsive shifts away from the biased region (p<10^-43), with stimuli above the bias shifted higher and stimuli below shifted lower, contradicting the minimal distance hypothesis.
evaluation: This negative result is strongly endorsed by reviewers. Reviewer 1 emphasizes 'the very convincing negative results' and states 'it demonstrates convincingly that traditional neural decoding models cannot explain percepts.' The editor similarly notes the manuscript 'demonstrates convincingly' the failure of traditional models. The statistical significance (p<10^-43) and consistency across decoding methods support this conclusion.

result: A two-layer feedforward model with local adaptation at synaptic connections and distributed spectral integration successfully reproduces both the repulsive shifts in pitch representation and the directional decoding effects. The model accounts for observed tuning curve changes, directional selectivity patterns, and the build-up of contextual effects in humans.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the modeling results as valid. Reviewer 1 notes 'subsequent analysis and modeling appear rigorous,' and Reviewer 2 states 'the methods seem sound and the conclusions warranted and carefully stated.' The model's ability to match multiple aspects of the data (tuning changes, directional effects, temporal dynamics) strengthens its credibility, though reviewers note uncertainty about whether it represents the actual mechanism (see below).

result: The authors conclude that contextual influences on perception may be encoded at the level of primary sensory cortices through basic neural response properties like adaptation and directional selectivity, rather than requiring higher-level cognitive processing.
evaluation: Reviewers express uncertainty about the broader implications. The editor notes 'the manuscript could be clearer on the wider implications,' and Reviewer 1 states 'beyond the very convincing negative results, it is less clear exactly what the conclusion is or what readers should take away from this study.' Reviewer 1 specifically asks 'does this study make predictions about how information from auditory cortex must be read out by downstream areas?' Reviewer 2 acknowledges this is 'an observational, rather than an interventional study, and therefore only able to identify plausible candidate mechanisms rather than making definitive identifications.'

result: Ferret auditory cortex neurons show diverse tuning properties to Shepard tones, including onset-type cells with broad tuning, sharply tuned cells (2-3 semitones halfwidth) with co-tuned onset and sustained responses, and offset-tuned cells. Many cells respond to single constituent tones while others integrate across multiple octave-spaced components.
evaluation: These characterization results are not specifically discussed by reviewers but fall under the general acceptance of the experimental methods. Reviewer 1 states 'experimental design and data collection appear to have been executed carefully,' and Reviewer 2 notes 'the methods seem sound.' The detailed characterization supports the subsequent decoding analyses.

result: The study collected single-unit recordings from 662 neurons in 7 awake ferrets and MEG recordings from 16 human subjects using carefully controlled Shepard tone sequences with systematic variation of bias length, timing, and pitch class. Humans performed a two-alternative forced choice task while ferrets listened passively.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the methodological approach without specific concerns. Reviewer 1 states 'experimental design and data collection appear to have been executed carefully. Subsequent analysis and modeling appear rigorous.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the methods seem sound' and 'I would rate the quality of this study as very high, and I do not have any major issues to raise.' The only minor suggestion is that 'it might be helpful to work a little bit more methods detail into the results section.'

result: Multiple decoding approaches (PCA-based dimensionality reduction and weighted population vector) produce consistent results showing circular organization of pitch class representation with high accuracy (r>0.995, >99% variance explained). The magnitude of repulsive shifts depends on bias length and decays with time constants of 0.92-1.1 seconds.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the decoding methodology. Reviewer 1 notes 'subsequent analysis and modeling appear rigorous,' and the consistency across multiple decoding methods strengthens the conclusions. The robustness testing with different dimensionality reduction techniques (including tSNE) supports the reliability of the findings.

result: Alternative model architectures without distributed activity or with only global adaptation fail to reproduce the observed repulsive shifts and tuning curve changes, demonstrating the necessity of local adaptation combined with distributed spectral integration.
evaluation: These control analyses are implicitly accepted as part of the rigorous modeling approach. Reviewer 1 states 'subsequent analysis and modeling appear rigorous,' and Reviewer 2 notes 'the methods seem sound.' The systematic comparison of model variants strengthens the mechanistic conclusions.

result: The model implementation used a sampling rate of 20 Hz, a population of 500 cells split equally among non-directional, upward-selective, and downward-selective cells, and non-parametric statistical tests throughout to avoid distributional assumptions.
evaluation: These technical details are accepted without comment as part of the overall sound methodology. Reviewer 1 notes 'subsequent analysis and modeling appear rigorous,' and Reviewer 2 states 'the methods seem sound.'
